analysis.one_liner: Restores lawsuits over toxic exposure discovered years after the polluting company's last act.
analysis.headline: A bill to let toxic-exposure victims sue even when contamination is discovered late died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The Supreme Court ruled in CTS Corp. v. Waldburger that a North Carolina deadline—the 'statute of repose'—bars lawsuits filed more than 10 years after a company's last act at a contaminated site, even if no one knew about the pollution yet. This one-page bill would have amended the federal toxic cleanup law so that those state deadlines could not cut off federal toxic-exposure claims before contamination is discovered [S2]. It was introduced by Senator Kay Hagan of North Carolina in June 2014, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never heard from again [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who lived or worked near contaminated sites—like residents around the CTS plant in Asheville, NC—and discovered illnesses or property damage years after the polluting activity ended. The bill would have let them sue in cases where a state repose deadline shut the courthouse door before anyone could have known about the contamination [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'statutes of repose' to the list of state deadlines that the federal toxic cleanup law (CERCLA) preempts, so a suit can be filed within the federal window that starts when the contamination is discovered [S3].

Reverses the effect of CTS Corp. v. Waldburger, where the Supreme Court held that CERCLA does not preempt North Carolina's 10-year statute of repose, which ran out regardless of when the contamination was discovered [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies and landowners facing cleanup and damages liability at old contaminated sites—chiefly manufacturing firms that left hazardous waste behind decades ago—and their insurers, who would face suits revived for older exposures [S2].

drawbacks.text: Defendants argued before the Supreme Court that statutes of repose exist to give a final cut-off, so businesses are not exposed to open-ended liability for decades-old, long-completed conduct.
The bill was one sentence of amendments with no committee record, no hearing, and no independent analysis of how many old sites or claims it would reopen, so its real-world reach is untested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people whose cancers or property damage surfaced more than 10 years after the pollution stopped, the stakes were concrete: the bill offered the only realistic path to court. The cost falls on companies that may have complied with the law of their era and now face revived claims; the deepest flaw is not the policy but that Congress never examined it—it died before anyone weighed the tradeoffs in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never moved—no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors—before the session ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kay Hagan (D-NC) introduced the bill on June 26, 2014, in direct response to the Supreme Court's CTS Corp. v. Waldburger decision about North Carolina's statute of repose [S1] [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the same day; that is the last action of any kind recorded [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended [S4] [S5].

Under the ruling the bill targeted, people exposed to contamination from a site like the former CTS plant in Asheville, NC remain barred from suing once the state's 10-year repose period runs out, even if they discovered the harm later [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies with historical contamination liabilities—like the defendants in the CTS case—and their insurers keep the state repose deadlines as a shield against late-discovered toxic-exposure suits. Residents near old contaminated sites gained nothing and remain without a remedy in covered cases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Former polluters; exposed residents got nothing

for.name: Sen. Kay Hagan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to overturn the CTS Corp. v. Waldburger outcome for North Carolina residents and referred matters no further than her committee referral.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing, no markup, no vote—leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action, it never qualified for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support was a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, so the partisan shape of the bill is unknown [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Manufacturers and industrial landowners with legacy contamination
industries.note: The bill would have revived exposure to damages suits for hazardous waste left behind decades ago, ending the finality that statutes of repose give companies whose old conduct is discovered late. For residents of contaminated areas, the industry's interest in a liability cut-off runs directly against their access to court.
Reopened older toxic-exposure claims would extend insurers' long-tail liability under old policies. Their interest in finality also runs against victims seeking compensation.
